title: Rat Hell — the Libby Prison tunnel escape of 1864
sources: Wikipedia: Libby Prison escape — Libby Prison, a former warehouse in Richmond, Virginia, held captured Union officers; the Confederates believed it inescapable and whitewashed the outer walls so lurking prisoners would stand out; the flooded, rat-infested eastern basement kitchen was closed off and known as 'Rat Hell'; led by Colonel Thomas E. Rose of the 77th Pennsylvania, officers removed a stove and chipped through a chimney to reach it; they dug with few proper tools while hundreds of rats ran over them; the dirt was hidden under two feet of straw, and one man stayed buried in the straw all day to conceal the tunnel; after 17 days they broke through under a tobacco shed in the yard of Kerr's Warehouse; on the night of 9 February 1864 they walked out into Richmond, Rose striding past a sentinel unchallenged; a stampede followed, and a guard joked that 'somebody's coffeepot' had upset; 109 escaped and the alarm was not raised for nearly twelve hours; following the North Star, 59 reached Union lines; Rose was caught by Confederate pickets minutes from the Union front at Williamsburg, returned to Libby and exchanged for a Confederate colonel on 30 April 1864.

Images (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / Library of Congress): Libby Prison stereographs; Harper's Weekly interior view (1863); David Gilmour Blythe's painting 'Libby Prison' (1863); the interior in 1891; Colonel Thomas E. Rose; 'The escaped refugees from the Libey Prison' (1864); a prisoner's letter of 14 February 1864
Archive film (public domain): D. W. Griffith, 'The House with Closed Shutters' (1910) and 'Swords and Hearts' (1911) — Civil War dramas, illustrative; a candle (CC0)
Music: The Battle Hymn of the Republic (slow), public domain

post.facebook:
In 1864, 109 Union officers escaped from a Confederate prison through a tunnel dug in a cellar full of rats.

Libby Prison in Richmond, Virginia, was an old warehouse packed with captured Union officers. The guards thought it was escape-proof — they even whitewashed the walls so anyone sneaking outside would stand out. But in the basement was a flooded, pitch-dark room crawling with rats that nobody wanted to enter: Rat Hell.

Colonel Thomas Rose and his men got in through a chimney behind a stove. Every night they dug with almost no tools while hundreds of rats ran over them, hiding the dirt under the straw — one man stayed buried in it all day to cover the hole. After 17 days the tunnel came up under a tobacco shed outside the prison. On 9 February 1864 they simply walked out into Richmond; Rose strolled right past a sentry. When the rest of the prison found out there was a stampede — a guard heard the racket and joked that somebody's coffeepot had tipped over.

109 men got out and nobody noticed for almost twelve hours. Following the North Star, 59 reached Union lines. Rose was caught minutes from the Union front and dragged back to Libby.

youtube.description:
In 1864, 109 Union officers escaped from a Confederate prison through a tunnel dug in a cellar full of rats.

Libby Prison in Richmond, Virginia, was thought to be escape-proof. Led by Colonel Thomas E. Rose of the 77th Pennsylvania, prisoners broke through a chimney into the flooded, rat-infested basement known as 'Rat Hell', hid the dirt under straw and, after 17 days of digging, came up under a tobacco shed outside the prison. On the night of 9 February 1864, 109 men walked out into Richmond; the alarm wasn't raised for nearly twelve hours, and 59 reached Union lines following the North Star. Rose himself was caught minutes from the Union front.
